courses.title: HTML from Zero to Advanced
courses.description: A complete HTML journey for curious readers, beginners, and engineering graduates, built to take a learner from raw markup to practical production-ready structure.

sections.label: Start here
sections.title: HTML is the foundation of every modern website.
sections.intro: If you are new to the web, this course is your complete HTML journey. We will move from the first tag to semantic architecture, accessibility, forms, media, and real-world page composition used in serious product teams.

cards.title: Who is this for?
cards.body: Readers, curious learners, engineering graduates, and anyone who wants to understand how websites truly work from the markup layer upward.

cards.title: What you will build
cards.body: By the end, you will understand how to write clean HTML for blogs, forms, dashboards, landing pages, and reusable content blocks.

cards.title: Why this matters
cards.body: Strong HTML is the difference between a page that looks okay and a page that is accessible, scalable, maintainable, and easy to extend.

visuals.code:
flowchart TD
A[Reader starts here] --> B[Learn HTML basics]
B --> C[Structure content]
C --> D[Build forms and layouts]
D --> E[Ship accessible, real pages]

paragraphs: This course is designed for people who do not just want to memorize tags, but want to understand why those tags exist and how they shape real experiences. A beautiful webpage is not only about design. It begins with clear content structure, accessible labels, and dependable semantics.

HTML is the skeleton of the web. It decides what information exists, what order it appears in, and how a browser interprets meaning. Without good HTML, CSS has very little context to work with, and JavaScript cannot reliably interact with a page that was not built with intention.

From a learner's perspective, the goal is simple: learn to read the structure, write it clearly, and build confidence through repetition. From a teacher's perspective, the challenge is to explain the why behind every tag so that students do not treat markup as random syntax. From a reader's perspective, the result should feel obvious, helpful, and trustworthy when the page loads.

That is why this course is built for readers and engineers. We want you to understand the reasoning behind each tag and to feel confident writing pages that are readable, maintainable, and production-ready.

sections.label: Lesson 1
sections.title: HTML basics: documents, tags, and structure.
sections.intro: Every webpage begins with a document structure. The browser reads HTML tags and converts them into meaningful content and layout.
list: The <!DOCTYPE html> declaration tells the browser the document type.
The <html> element is the root of every HTML document.
The <head> contains metadata, title, and SEO information.
The <body> contains the actual content users read and interact with.
A clean HTML document is easier to debug, SEO-friendly, and much easier to extend later.
Common beginner mistake: writing content without a proper structure, which makes the page harder to read and harder to style.
paragraphs: The first skill in HTML is understanding the document model. Think of a web page as a structured tree. The browser parses tags and creates a page hierarchy that organizes headings, paragraphs, links, images, and interactive controls.

The most important idea here is that HTML is not just a random set of text. It is a semantic language. When you write a page, you are telling the browser which pieces of the content are primary headings, which pieces are paragraph text, and which pieces are navigation or form controls. That structure creates meaning, which improves accessibility and makes future CSS and JavaScript easier to apply correctly.

A good mental model is this: the browser reads your HTML and turns it into a DOM tree, a structured representation of the page. Your job as a developer is to write tags that describe the meaning of the content, not just the look. When you structure the document correctly, the browser, search engines, assistive technologies, and future code all understand the page better.

If you want to build a strong foundation, begin with a simple HTML document and keep it clean. A well-structured page is easier to debug, easier to scale, and much easier for other developers to maintain.

sections.label: Lesson 2
sections.title: Text content and semantic headings.
sections.intro: Readable web pages are built with well-structured text. Headings, paragraphs, emphasis, and quotes help users quickly understand the story of the page.
list: H1 is the primary page heading and should appear once per page.
H2 and H3 create a content hierarchy and improve readability.
Strong and em add emphasis without altering meaning.
Blockquotes and code tags show examples, citations, and technical snippets clearly.
paragraphs: Once the document structure is in place, the next step is content and hierarchy. A webpage is not just a wall of text. It is a collection of ideas arranged so that readers can scan, understand, and remember the information quickly.

Headings establish importance. A strong heading hierarchy tells the user where they are and what matters most. The main idea of the page belongs in an h1, while supporting ideas should be grouped under h2 and h3. This also helps assistive technology understand the structure and read content in a meaningful sequence.

Text styling in HTML is not only cosmetic. Strong emphasis, blockquotes, and code blocks are meaningful markup. They help readers understand hierarchy and intent without changing the content itself. In other words, these elements are as much about communication as they are about appearance.

A common mistake is to choose heading tags based only on visual size. Good HTML should reflect meaning, not just font appearance. The reader does not care whether you used a larger font manually; they care whether the page clearly communicates what is most important and what comes next.

sections.label: Lesson 3
sections.title: Links, images, and media elements.
sections.intro: Links connect pages, ideas, and resources. Media elements allow websites to tell richer stories and deliver information in more engaging ways.
list: Anchor tags create navigation and references to other pages or sections.
Image tags communicate visual context and should include alt text.
The src attribute loads the media resource, while alt describes it for accessibility.
Video and audio tags let you embed content directly inside the document.
paragraphs: Links are the glue of the web. Without them, pages would exist in isolation. An anchor tag can send the user to another page, a section on the same page, or even a different part of the same document. This is the reason navigation systems work the way they do and why readers can move from one concept to the next without confusion.

Images are equally important. They are not decoration only. They can convey meaning, add visual examples, and clarify a process. However, accessibility matters. Every meaningful image should ideally include alt text. This helps users with assistive technology or slow connections understand what the image is trying to tell them.

Media elements like video, audio, and figures make a page richer and more practical. When used well, they support explanations instead of overwhelming the reader. Good HTML treats media as supporting evidence, not as noise.

sections.label: Lesson 4
sections.title: Lists, tables, and meaningful content grouping.
sections.intro: Real content often needs grouping. Lists and tables are used when we need to present steps, product features, results, or structured information.
list: Unordered lists are good for a group of ideas without sequence.
Ordered lists are excellent for step-by-step instructions or process flow.
Tables work best for information that must be compared row by row.
A table should still maintain a readable structure and be used only when data is tabular.
paragraphs: As the amount of information grows, the need for structure becomes more obvious. Lists help organize steps, checklists, feature summaries, and reading paths. Ordered lists help create a sequence of actions, while unordered lists help communicate related ideas without implying a strict order.

Tables are a different challenge. They are valuable when you need to compare or track values, but they should not be used for layout. A table is a data structure, not a design tool. If the content is not tabular, use sections and divs instead.

Good grouping makes pages easier to read and much easier to maintain. A learner who can scan the page quickly understands the ideas faster and is more likely to remember the structure and logic behind the content.

sections.label: Lesson 5
sections.title: Forms: inputs, buttons, labels, and real user interaction.
sections.intro: Forms are where static pages become interactive tools. They are essential for sign-ups, contact pages, search, feedback collection, and structured user input.
list: Labels improve accessibility and help users understand what field they are filling.
Input types include text, email, password, number, date, and search.
Button elements trigger form submission or action events.
Fieldsets group related inputs together for better structure and readability.
paragraphs: Forms are one of the most practical parts of HTML because they connect the page to real user interaction. A contact form, search box, registration form, or login page all rely on form elements working together correctly. Without the right fields, labels, and structure, the form becomes confusing and inaccessible.

A well-designed form is more than a row of inputs. It is a conversation between the user and the system. Labels tell the user what to type, placeholders help guide them, and the correct input types help browsers validate better before the data even reaches the backend.

This is also a critical place for engineering discipline. A form should be easy to understand, consistent in design, accessible by keyboard, and built with semantics that future developers can maintain. Good forms reduce friction and increase trust.
codeBlocks:
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Student information</legend>

    <label for="name">Name</label>
    <input id="name" name="name" type="text" placeholder="Enter your name" required />

    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required />

    <button type="submit">Join course</button>
  </fieldset>
</form>

sections.label: Lesson 6
sections.title: Semantic HTML and accessibility for real users.
sections.intro: Accessible HTML helps screen readers, keyboard users, and all kinds of users understand your page. Good semantics create a better experience for everyone.
list: header, main, nav, section, article, aside, and footer are semantic landmarks.
aria-label helps describe interactive elements when plain text is not enough.
Alt text is required for meaningful images and helpful for screen reader users.
Using semantic structure improves clarity, SEO, maintainability, and developer collaboration.
paragraphs: Accessibility is not an extra feature. It is part of good engineering. A page that is structured semantically and labeled correctly works better for keyboard users, screen readers, and users with low bandwidth or visual limitations. It also improves SEO because search engines understand the page structure more clearly.

Semantic HTML gives meaning to the code itself. Instead of using generic containers everywhere, we use elements that describe the role of the content. A nav tells the browser that this block is navigation, a main block defines the primary content, and an article can represent a stand-alone piece of information.

When you write semantic HTML, you are not just making pages prettier. You are making them clearer for both browsers and humans. This is one of the strongest engineering habits you can build early in your web journey.

sections.label: Lesson 7
sections.title: Page structure and layout patterns used in real websites.
sections.intro: A strong web page is more than just content. It uses structure to create readable, scalable, and maintainable page layouts that feel intentional.
list: header holds branding, nav, and primary actions.
main contains the primary content of the page.
aside is useful for related information or side content.
footer contains utility links, policies, and contact information.
paragraphs: When developers talk about layout, they are often referring to how content is grouped. A good layout is not just a visual balance between blocks. It is a structure that helps users understand the story of the page and find important information quickly. Real websites use clear sections for hero content, features, testimonials, navigation, and calls to action.

HTML gives the layout its semantic shape. The way you group content decides whether your page feels coherent or cluttered. A strong page usually has a header, a main content area, optional supporting sidebars, and a footer. These landmarks create a predictable mental model that users and developers both understand quickly.

This is the bridge between raw markup and front-end design. Once your HTML structure is semantically sound, CSS becomes easier to apply and JavaScript becomes easier to integrate. You are building a foundation for future complexity, not just drawing boxes on the screen.

sections.label: Lesson 8
sections.title: Advanced HTML patterns: validation, metadata, and production-ready structure.
sections.intro: Advanced HTML is about building pages that are maintainable, searchable, accessible, and ready for real deployment. This is where quality engineering habits begin.
list: Meta tags help describe page purpose, keywords, and social sharing previews.
Input validation rules reduce bad data and improve user experience.
Semantic HTML supports accessibility, future code changes, and stronger SEO.
Good structure makes the page easier to extend with CSS and JavaScript later.
paragraphs: Once you understand the basics, the next level is quality. Production-grade HTML is not only about syntax correctness. It is about predictable structure, clean semantics, and consistent use of metadata. This becomes especially important when pages begin to scale and when multiple developers contribute to the same project.

Meta tags help browsers and social platforms understand the page purpose. The title, viewport metadata, description, and canonical tags all influence how the page is presented in search and on social sharing sites. Good metadata is part of product quality, not an optional add-on.

Validation rules also matter. Inputs with required, min, max, type, and pattern attributes help reduce mistakes before the data reaches the backend. This is a good example of how HTML contributes to real-world user experience and engineering discipline.
codeBlocks:
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8" />
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
  <meta name="description" content="Learn HTML from beginner to advanced with practical examples." />
  <title>HTML Course</title>
</head>

<input type="email" name="email" required />
<input type="number" min="18" max="100" />

sections.label: Lesson 9
sections.title: Build a realistic landing page with clean HTML.
sections.intro: The best way to master HTML is to create something realistic. A landing page is one of the most useful beginner-to-advanced exercises because it combines many commonly used elements in one complete design.
list: A landing page needs clear hero text, trust signals, feature sections, and a call to action.
Good HTML groups related content into logical sections instead of dumping everything into one block.
Reusable patterns make the structure easier to scale with CSS and future content.
Strong markup creates a foundation for responsive design and engineering-quality front-end work.
paragraphs: This final core lesson is about synthesis. Instead of learning isolated tags in a vacuum, you now combine them into a coherent product page. A landing page requires a clear headline, some explanatory copy, feature blocks, and form or CTA elements. The stronger your HTML structure, the easier it will be to layer in CSS and JavaScript later.

This is also where the real-world mindset kicks in. Good front-end developers think in sections, components, and content hierarchy. They do not just place elements because they fit on a viewport. They organize them to help the user understand the value of the product and take the next step.
If you can build a landing page cleanly with HTML, you are already thinking like a front-end engineer. The next steps in CSS and JavaScript become much easier because the foundation is strong.

courses.title: SQL Essentials
courses.description: A graduate-level SQL journey designed as 30-minute reading lessons with theory, examples, and hands-on SQL practice for real engineering work.

sections.label: Start here
sections.title: SQL for engineering graduates.
sections.intro: SQL is the language of data. Whether you are building applications, dashboards, data pipelines, or internal tools, SQL is the common language that turns raw records into decisions. This course is designed as focused 30-minute lessons so a learner can build real understanding without overwhelm.

cards.title: What is SQL?
cards.body: SQL stands for Structured Query Language and lets you define, query, transform, and manage relational data in a clear and repeatable way.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.body: Modern product teams, backend engineers, analysts, and data teams all depend on SQL for reporting, business logic, and operational decision-making.

cards.title: What you will build
cards.body: You will learn how to model tables, query real datasets, join related records, analyze trends, and write production-safe SQL.

sections.label: Lesson 1
sections.title: Database fundamentals and the relational model
sections.intro: A relational database stores information in tables. Each table represents a concept such as students, courses, orders, or employees, and the relationships between them define the system. This is the foundation of every serious SQL workflow.
list: Entity: a real-world thing or concept such as Student, Course, or Account.
Attribute: a property of that entity such as name, salary, or date joined.
Table: a collection of related records described by columns.
Primary key: a unique identifier for every row.
Foreign key: a column that references data in another table.
Normalization: organizing data to reduce duplication and improve consistency.
paragraphs: The relational model is one of the most important ideas in software engineering. Instead of storing everything in one giant list, we split data into smaller, connected tables. This makes the system easier to reason about, easier to query, and easier to maintain as the business grows.

Think of a table as a spreadsheet with a strict structure. The columns define what kind of information is stored, and each row represents one record. A primary key tells us which record is unique, while a foreign key connects two tables together. This relationship is what lets us answer richer questions like 'which student enrolled in which course?' or 'which employee belongs to which department?'.

Good data design is not only a technical detail; it protects the quality of the entire product. Poor table design leads to redundant records, inconsistent values, and difficult query logic. That is why engineers spend time thinking carefully about entities, keys, and relationships before writing a single query.

editor.label: Schema explorer
editor.defaultQuery: SELECT s.name, COUNT(e.course_id) AS courses_enrolled FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.student_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.name ORDER BY courses_enrolled DESC;
editor.schema: CREATE TABLE students (student_id INTEGER, name TEXT, department TEXT, year_of_study INTEGER); CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INTEGER, course_name TEXT, credits INTEGER); CREATE TABLE enrollments (student_id INTEGER, course_id INTEGER, grade TEXT);
seedQueries: INSERT INTO students (student_id, name, department, year_of_study) VALUES (1, 'Aarav', 'CS', 2);
INSERT INTO students (student_id, name, department, year_of_study) VALUES (2, 'Nisha', 'ECE', 3);
INSERT INTO students (student_id, name, department, year_of_study) VALUES (3, 'Kabir', 'CS', 2);
INSERT INTO courses (course_id, course_name, credits) VALUES (101, 'DBMS', 4);
INSERT INTO courses (course_id, course_name, credits) VALUES (102, 'Algorithms', 3);
INSERT INTO enrollments (student_id, course_id, grade) VALUES (1, 101, 'A');
INSERT INTO enrollments (student_id, course_id, grade) VALUES (1, 102, 'B');
INSERT INTO enrollments (student_id, course_id, grade) VALUES (3, 101, 'A');

sections.label: Lesson 2
sections.title: DDL: define schema and enforce data integrity
sections.intro: DDL stands for Data Definition Language. It is how you create, alter, and remove tables and constraints. This matters because schema design defines how safe and reliable your data will be over time.
list: CREATE TABLE creates a new table structure.
ALTER TABLE modifies the existing table definition.
DROP TABLE removes a table permanently.
PRIMARY KEY enforces uniqueness for row identity.
FOREIGN KEY protects relationships across tables.
CHECK, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and DEFAULT improve data quality.
paragraphs: The schema is the blueprint of your database. It tells SQL what the data should look like before any business logic runs. A strong schema reduces bugs because invalid values are rejected early rather than being allowed to spread through the application.

This is where database engineering becomes disciplined and professional. Constraints are not decoration; they are rules. A NOT NULL constraint prevents missing values, CHECK ensures valid ranges, UNIQUE prevents duplicates, and foreign keys protect relationships. These rules are part of the product's data guarantee.

When someone says 'the data is clean,' they usually mean the database has a solid schema behind it. SQL gives you the tools to define that structure clearly, and a disciplined engineer uses them intentionally.

editor.label: Schema validation
editor.schema: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, department TEXT NOT NULL, salary INTEGER CHECK (salary >= 0), age INTEGER CHECK (age >= 18), city TEXT DEFAULT 'Unknown');
seedQueries: INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, age, city) VALUES (1, 'Aarav', 'Engineering', 90000, 28, 'Pune');
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, age, city) VALUES (2, 'Nisha', 'Marketing', 72000, 26, 'Delhi');
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, age, city) VALUES (3, 'Kabir', 'Engineering', 85000, 30, 'Bengaluru');

sections.label: Lesson 3
sections.title: DML: insert, update, delete, and maintain records
sections.intro: DML stands for Data Manipulation Language. This is where data enters, changes, and leaves the system. A database is only useful when it can represent real business activity accurately.
list: INSERT adds new rows to a table.
UPDATE changes values in existing rows.
DELETE removes rows that are no longer needed.
SELECT reads or filters rows for questions and analysis.
Transactions bundle operations so they either all succeed or all fail.
paragraphs: Good SQL engineers think in terms of safe data changes. An update can accidentally affect too many rows if the WHERE condition is wrong, and a delete without a filter can remove the wrong data. That is why careful query writing matters so much in data work.

Transactions are the safety net. Imagine transferring money from one account to another: if the debit succeeds but the credit fails, the financial records are wrong. SQL transactions help ensure that changes happen as a single atomic unit. That is one of the most important ideas in database reliability.
This lesson teaches you how to manage records responsibly. The goal is not just to write queries, but to write queries that preserve correctness and reflect business intent.

editor.label: Record operations
editor.defaultQuery: SELECT employee_id, name, department, salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC;
editor.schema: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, department TEXT, salary INTEGER, age INTEGER);
seedQueries: INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, age) VALUES (1, 'Aarav', 'Engineering', 90000, 28);
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, age) VALUES (2, 'Nisha', 'Marketing', 72000, 26);
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, age) VALUES (3, 'Kabir', 'Engineering', 85000, 30);
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, age) VALUES (4, 'Meera', 'Design', 76000, 24);

sections.label: Lesson 4
sections.title: SELECT: filter, sort, and shape results
sections.intro: The SELECT statement is the heart of SQL. It is how you ask questions of the database and shape the answer into something usable. This is the lesson that turns raw records into insight.
list: SELECT lists the columns you want to see.
FROM tells SQL which table to read from.
WHERE filters rows using conditions.
ORDER BY sorts rows in ascending or descending order.
LIMIT restricts the number of rows returned.
DISTINCT removes duplicate rows.
LIKE supports pattern-based matching.
paragraphs: Every serious SQL workflow starts with SELECT. The first question is usually not 'how do I join tables?' but 'what data am I actually trying to read?' Querying well means choosing the right columns, filtering to the relevant rows, and making the answer easy to understand.

Many beginner mistakes happen here: selecting too many columns, forgetting the WHERE clause, or sorting the wrong field. These mistakes are easy to make when you are learning, but they become costly in production data work. A good SQL engineer gets the question, writes the intent clearly, and validates the output before moving ahead.

This is also where SQL starts to feel like a language of reasoning. You are not just reading data; you are answering a business question. 'Which customers bought in the last thirty days?' 'Which engineers earn above the department average?' These are real analytical prompts, and SELECT is how you answer them.
codeBlocks:
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 80000
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 5;

SELECT DISTINCT city
FROM employees
WHERE city LIKE 'P%';

editor.label: Query builder
editor.defaultQuery: SELECT name, department, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 75000 ORDER BY salary DESC;
editor.schema: CREATE TABLE employees (employee_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, department TEXT, salary INTEGER, city TEXT);
seedQueries: INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, city) VALUES (1, 'Aarav', 'Engineering', 90000, 'Pune');
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, city) VALUES (2, 'Nisha', 'Marketing', 72000, 'Delhi');
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, city) VALUES (3, 'Kabir', 'Engineering', 85000, 'Bengaluru');
INSERT INTO employees (employee_id, name, department, salary, city) VALUES (4, 'Meera', 'Design', 76000, 'Mumbai');

sections.label: Lesson 5
sections.title: Aggregations and grouping for real analysis
sections.intro: A lot of SQL work is not about individual rows; it is about summarizing them. Aggregation gives you the tools to calculate totals, averages, counts, and patterns across large datasets.
list: COUNT counts the number of rows or non-null values.
SUM adds numeric values.
AVG calculates the average value.
MIN and MAX return the smallest and largest values.
GROUP BY organizes rows into groups.
HAVING filters aggregated groups.
paragraphs: Aggregation is where SQL stops being a lookup language and starts being a reporting language. You can answer questions like 'How many users signed up this month?' 'What is the average salary by department?' or 'Which products are generating the most revenue?'. These are essential business questions, and SQL is built for them.

One of the most important rules in aggregation is understanding the difference between WHERE and HAVING. WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, while HAVING filters the grouped results after aggregation. A clear understanding of this difference is a hallmark of a strong SQL developer.
As you grow in SQL, you will realize that most real dashboard queries depend on grouping and aggregation. It is one of the most practical and important parts of the language.
codeBlocks:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS employee_count, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 75000
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

sections.label: Lesson 6
sections.title: Joins: connect related tables and answer deeper questions
sections.intro: Most real systems require more than one table. Joins allow us to combine related information so we can answer richer business questions without duplicating data.
list: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables.
LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the left table and matches where possible.
RIGHT JOIN keeps all rows from the right table.
FULL OUTER JOIN keeps unmatched rows from both sides.
Self-join compares values within the same table.
paragraphs: A normalized database splits related data across multiple tables, but the business problem is often asked across those tables at once. Joins are how SQL reconnects that data in a meaningful way. Without joins, the data system would feel fragmented and every query would need manual merging logic.

The choice of join type matters. An INNER JOIN is useful when you only care about records with matching relationships. A LEFT JOIN is often the safer default when you want every parent record and the optional related records. If you do not understand the difference, you can quickly misread the data and produce incorrect reporting.
This is a core skill for engineers, analysts, and product teams. In real business work, the interesting questions almost always involve more than one table, so join logic is essential.
codeBlocks:
SELECT e.name, d.department_name, e.salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.department_id
WHERE e.salary > 80000;

SELECT c.course_name, s.name
FROM courses c
LEFT JOIN enrollments en ON c.course_id = en.course_id
LEFT JOIN students s ON s.student_id = en.student_id;

sections.label: Lesson 7
sections.title: Subqueries, CTEs, and set logic
sections.intro: Subqueries and CTEs let you break large problems into smaller logical steps. They help you answer questions that need layered filtering, derived data, or reusable logic.
list: Subquery: a query inside another query.
IN and EXISTS help check whether records match a condition.
CTE: a temporary named result used to simplify complex reads.
UNION combines results from multiple queries.
INTERSECT and EXCEPT compare sets of rows.
paragraphs: Sometimes the business question is not just 'show me some rows,' but 'show me rows that satisfy a condition based on another calculation.' That is where subqueries shine. They let you compute an intermediate result and then use it as input to a larger question.

CTEs are especially useful when queries become long and hard to read. Instead of burying a complex logic tree in one giant statement, you can name the intermediate stages and make the logic readable. This is a strong engineering habit because maintainable SQL is readable SQL.

Set operations are another powerful idea. UNION allows you to stack answers together, while INTERSECT and EXCEPT help you compare collections precisely. These are valuable tools for analytical reporting and data reconciliation.

sections.label: Lesson 8
sections.title: Window functions for ranking and running analysis
sections.intro: Window functions let you compute values across a set of rows without collapsing the result set. This is what makes SQL powerful for dashboards, scoring, ranking, and trend analysis.
list: ROW_NUMBER assigns a unique sequence within a result set.
RANK and DENSE_RANK handle ties in rankings.
SUM OVER computes running or grouped totals.
PARTITION BY splits the calculation by a category.
ORDER BY inside the window defines the calculation sequence.
paragraphs: Window functions are one of the most important advanced SQL concepts because they bridge the gap between simple filtering and data analysis. Instead of reducing rows to one summary, window functions allow us to calculate values row by row while still retaining the full dataset.

This is especially useful for leaderboards, cumulative totals, monthly trends, and risk scoring. If you have ever wanted to know 'what was the running total after each order?' or 'who ranks first in each department?', window functions are the tool for that job.

The key idea is that the function operates over a set of rows while preserving the original result. This is a very different mental model from aggregate queries, and once understood, it unlocks a major portion of analytical SQL.

editor.label: Window function lab
editor.defaultQuery: SELECT name, department, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dept_rank FROM employees ORDER BY department, dept_rank;

sections.label: Lesson 9
sections.title: Performance tuning: indexes, execution plans, and query quality
sections.intro: A query that returns the correct answer is useful, but a query that returns the correct answer quickly is production-ready. Performance tuning is about understanding how SQL executes work under the hood.
list: Indexes speed up reads for frequent lookups and filters.
EXPLAIN shows how the database plans a query.
Avoid selecting unnecessary columns or rows.
Poor join patterns and missing indexes often create slow queries.
Query clarity matters because readable SQL is usually easier to optimize.
paragraphs: When people talk about SQL performance, they often talk about indexes. An index is like a book index: it helps the database find the right rows faster. But indexes are not free. They improve read speed and can slow down writes, so they must be chosen with care.

Execution plans help you understand what the database is doing. A query may look simple, but the planner might scan a massive table or perform repeated work. That is why experienced engineers learn to read EXPLAIN output and understand where the time is being spent.
This lesson is about engineering judgment. Performance is not just a technical metric; it affects product responsiveness, cost, and the overall experience of the application.

sections.label: Practice
sections.title: Capstone SQL challenge
sections.intro: This final practice is designed to feel like a real business task. You will combine filtering, grouping, joins, and aggregate logic to answer a data-driven question from a realistic scenario.
sections.challenge: Find the departments whose average salary is above the overall average, then show the employee count and average salary in each qualifying department.
paragraphs: This challenge is not about memorizing syntax. It is about applying the thinking you learned across the course. You need to understand grouping, conditional filtering, and the difference between aggregate and row-level logic. That is where SQL skills become real problem-solving skills.

The strongest SQL programmers do not just write queries; they read a question, identify the data model, plan the join or aggregation logic, and validate the output. This final exercise is designed to help you practice that workflow in a realistic and repeatable way.

sections.label: Start here
sections.title: System design is the skill of turning vague product ideas into scalable architecture.
sections.intro: This course is built around the same mindset as a strong engineering book: theory first, then examples, then trade-offs, then implementation patterns you can reuse in interviews and real systems.

cards.title: Who is this for?
cards.body: Engineers preparing for interviews, product-minded developers, and curious builders who want to reason about scale, data flow, and bottlenecks with confidence.

cards.title: What you will learn
cards.body: How to translate a vague requirement into a real architecture, estimate load, select storage layers, and defend design trade-offs clearly.

cards.title: Why this matters
cards.body: Modern systems are not built by memorizing buzzwords. They are built by understanding constraints, failure modes, and the right place to add complexity.

visuals.code:
flowchart TD
A[Product idea] --> B[Scope the problem]
B --> C[Estimate load]
C --> D[Choose services and storage]
D --> E[Design for growth]
E --> F[Defend trade-offs]

paragraphs: A system design interview is rarely about writing a perfect diagram. It is about showing that you can think clearly under uncertainty. The best answers begin with constraints, clarify assumptions, and then build a system that can handle real traffic and failure conditions.

This course follows a book-like learning flow: concept first, architecture next, real-world examples after that, and then implementation patterns that you can reuse across chat systems, feeds, search services, and file platforms.
The goal is not to memorize a fixed answer for one product. The goal is to build a reusable mental model so that every new architecture problem feels structured instead of chaotic.

sections.label: Lesson 1
sections.title: Scale from zero to millions of users
sections.intro: Every scalable system begins as a simple one-server design. The real engineering skill is knowing when to add load balancers, caches, queues, and replicated storage without overengineering the system.
list: A single app server and one database work well for early product growth.
Load balancers help distribute traffic when one process is no longer enough.
A cache is a performance multiplier when repeated reads are expensive.
Queues move non-critical work out of the request path and into background processing.
Horizontal scaling is useful only when the architecture and traffic pattern justify it.
paragraphs: A common mistake is to jump from a single database to a distributed architecture before there is real evidence that the system needs it. In early stages, simplicity is a strength. It reduces debugging time, lowers operational risk, and makes the product easier to ship.

As users increase, bottlenecks appear: request volume, CPU usage, database pressure, and storage limits. That is when engineers introduce separation of concerns: stateless app servers, read replicas, caches, and asynchronous background workers.
This lesson teaches a simple rule: scale only when your traffic and product behavior demand it. A good architecture grows in layers, not in leaps.

visuals.code:
flowchart LR
A[User traffic] --> B[One web server]
B --> C[One database]
C --> D[Load balancer]
D --> E[Multiple app instances]
E --> F[Cache]
F --> G[Async workers]

codeBlocks:
# A simple request path
GET /feed -> app server -> database -> response

# When traffic grows
GET /feed -> load balancer -> app server -> cache
app server -> database only on cache miss
background workers process heavy updates asynchronously

sections.label: Lesson 2
sections.title: Requirements, constraints, and non-functional goals
sections.intro: Every design begins with a requirement. The difference between a good and a weak system design is whether the team can separate functional needs from performance and reliability expectations.
list: Functional requirements explain what the system should do.
Non-functional expectations define speed, availability, durability, and consistency.
Constraints limit the design: traffic, latency targets, data size, and operational budget.
Good design means choosing trade-offs that match product reality.
paragraphs: A vague prompt like “Design WhatsApp” or “Design a social feed” is not a design. It is the starting point for a requirements conversation. You need to ask questions: how many users, what percentage are active, how many writes per second, how much latency is acceptable, and what kind of failures are tolerated.

Functional requirements answer the question, “what does the system do?” Non-functional requirements answer, “how should it behave under pressure?” An API can be correct but still unusable if latency is poor, availability is fragile, or writes are inconsistent.
That is why a strong architect begins by clarifying scope and constraints before drawing components. It is the difference between building a diagram and designing a real system.

visuals.code:
flowchart TD
A[Product prompt] --> B[Functional requirements]
A --> C[Non-functional goals]
B --> D[Core features]
C --> E[Latency, durability, scale]
D --> F[Architecture choices]
E --> F

codeBlocks:
Example requirement breakdown

Functional:
- users can create posts
- users can read timelines
- users can follow others

Non-functional:
- p95 read latency < 200 ms
- data retention for 2 years
- 99.9% availability
- eventual consistency for feed updates is acceptable

sections.label: Lesson 3
sections.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
sections.intro: System design is not only about diagrams. It is about converting rough assumptions into numbers that help you pick the right storage, serving layer, and traffic strategy.
list: Estimate daily active users and requests per second.
Calculate write volume and storage growth.
Model read-heavy vs write-heavy workloads.
Use numbers to justify architecture, not to chase precision.
paragraphs: Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a communication skill. It turns vague product ideas into credible architecture decisions. If a system expects 100,000 writes per second, then the storage layer, network plan, and queue design all change.

A strong estimate is not perfect, but it should be explainable. You can say: “Assume 1 million daily active users, 2 reads per session, average payload 2 KB, and 20% write traffic. That means approximately X requests per second and Y storage growth per month.” That is where design confidence starts.
This lesson is about reducing uncertainty. The result is not a spreadsheet answer but a better mental model for discussing what the system must handle.
codeBlocks:
# Example estimation for a social feed
DAU = 10 million
Reads per user per day = 30
Writes per user per day = 2
Average post size = 2 KB

Total reads/day = 300M
Total writes/day = 20M
Storage/year = 20M * 2KB * 365 ~= 14.6 TB (before compression and redundancy)

sections.label: Lesson 4
sections.title: A framework for system design interviews
sections.intro: A repeatable framework keeps large, open-ended problems manageable. You do not need a perfect design on the first pass; you need a structured design process that makes sense to the interviewer.
list: Clarify problem scope and product assumptions.
Capture functional and non-functional requirements.
Estimate traffic and data volume.
Choose a high-level architecture.
Identify bottlenecks and propose iterative improvements.
paragraphs: The interview answer should feel organized. Start by clarifying the problem, then define constraints, then move into architecture. After that, explain trade-offs and what would change under heavier load.

A common weakness is starting with a giant component list instead of first understanding the user flow. The better flow is: service boundaries, data movement, storage decisions, read/write optimization, and failure handling.
This lesson gives you a mental checklist you can reuse across URL shorteners, notification systems, file platforms, chat apps, or search engines.

visuals.code:
flowchart TD
A[Understand problem] --> B[Scope requirements]
B --> C[Estimate load]
C --> D[Define architecture]
D --> E[Find bottlenecks]
E --> F[Improve the design]
F --> G[Explain trade-offs]

codeBlocks:
Design checklist
1. Clarify requirements
2. Define traffic and storage
3. Choose key services
4. Decide on databases and caching
5. Model read/write flows
6. Discuss failures, scaling, and trade-offs

sections.label: Lesson 5
sections.title: Storage, schema design, and the data model
sections.intro: Storage decisions shape the entire system. A database is not just a place to store rows—it defines access patterns, write cost, consistency, and operational complexity.
list: SQL is strong for relational data, joins, and transactional correctness.
NoSQL is often better when scalability and flexible schemas dominate the design.
Object storage is ideal for large files and media assets.
The database choice should follow the workload, not the hype.
paragraphs: A relational database is a good fit when you have strong relationships, predictable queries, and a need for transactions. A document or key-value store can be better when the data is high-volume, semi-structured, or write-heavy.
The architecture of a feed, a search index, a chat history table, and a file storage system are all different. Each product has its own access pattern and therefore its own storage design.
This lesson is about making the right trade-off. The right storage design reduces complexity and helps the system behave predictably under load.

visuals.code:
erDiagram
USER ||--o{ POST : creates
USER ||--o{ FOLLOW : follows
POST }o--|| USER : authored

sections.label: Lesson 6
sections.title: Caching, read optimization, and invalidation
sections.intro: Caching is one of the most practical ways to reduce latency and database load. But cached data introduces correctness problems if invalidation and freshness are poorly managed.
list: Cache hot reads close to the application layer.
Use CDNs for static assets and media.
Apply TTLs, cache-aside patterns, and write-through strategies carefully.
Weak invalidation logic creates stale data and broken product behavior.
paragraphs: A cache works because repeated reads are expensive. If the same product data is requested thousands of times per second, a cache can reduce load by serving the result from memory instead of querying the database again.

The complexity is in invalidation. If a user updates a profile, the cache may still hold old data. The design must decide whether stale data is acceptable, how quickly it should refresh, and when writes must invalidate prior reads.
This lesson teaches that optimization must respect correctness. The fastest design is not the best design if it produces stale, inconsistent, or confusing responses.

visuals.code:
flowchart LR
A[Request] --> B{Cache hit?}
B -->|Yes| C[Serve fast]
B -->|No| D[Read DB]
D --> E[Write cache]
E --> F[Return response]

codeBlocks:
# Cache-aside pattern
value = cache.get(key)
if value is None:
    value = db.get(key)
    cache.set(key, value, ttl=60)
return value

# On write:
update_db(key, new_value)
cache.delete(key) # invalidate stale data

sections.label: Lesson 7
sections.title: Consistency models, CAP, and distributed trade-offs
sections.intro: Distributed systems cannot maximize every property at once. A strong architecture chooses the right consistency and availability model for the business problem.
list: Consistency defines how fresh reads are after a write.
Availability measures how often the system keeps serving traffic during failures.
Partition tolerance is a reality in distributed systems, even when we prefer not to think about it.
CAP helps explain why systems often choose a trade-off instead of trying to have everything.
paragraphs: CAP is a conceptual model, not a magical law. It reminds us that when a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between strong consistency and continued availability for some operations.

That trade-off depends on the product. A payments system may prefer strong consistency. A feed or social timeline may be okay with eventual consistency if the UX remains acceptable. The key is not to pretend the trade-off does not exist.
This lesson teaches you to explain the choice in business terms: what users experience, what risks are tolerated, and what costs each model imposes.

visuals.code:
flowchart TB
A[Distributed system] --> B[Consistency]
A --> C[Availability]
A --> D[Partition tolerance]
B --> E[Strong guarantees]
C --> F[Keep serving users]
D --> G[Network failure is inevitable]

codeBlocks:
Strong consistency example
- bank transfer updates account balances atomically
- read-after-write guarantees matter

Eventual consistency example
- social feed may show latest posts slightly delayed
- users still get a useful experience without downtime

sections.label: Lesson 8
sections.title: Distributed patterns: rate limiting, hashing, IDs, and URL shorteners
sections.intro: Many classic interview problems are really exercises in routing, partitioning, and safe scalability. They appear again and again because they teach fundamental design skills.
list: Rate limiting protects backend services from abuse and spikes.
Consistent hashing reduces rebalancing when nodes are added or removed.
Unique ID generation must avoid collisions and coordination bottlenecks.
A URL shortener is a compact system design challenge that combines storage, redirect logic, and scale concerns.
paragraphs: Rate limiting is a service boundary problem. It decides whether one user, one tenant, or one API consumer is allowed to generate too much traffic. It protects downstream systems and keeps user experience fair and predictable.

Consistent hashing matters when data is distributed across many machines. It gives a predictable mapping between keys and nodes, which is critical for partitioned stores and large-scale service topologies.

IDs may seem simple, but at scale they are a distributed coordination problem. A good design uses a clearly defined generation strategy and avoids collisions, sequencing issues, and application-level surprises.
codeBlocks:
# Rate limiter idea
if requests_per_minute(user_id) > limit:
    reject_with_429()
else:
    allow_request()

# Consistent hash example
node_ring = [n1, n2, n3, n4]
key_hash = hash(user_id)
route_to_nearest_node(key_hash, node_ring)

# Short URL: id -> long_url mapping
short_code = encode(id)
redirect(short_code) -> original_url

sections.label: Lesson 9
sections.title: Feeds, chat, search, and product-scale systems
sections.intro: The most valuable system design problems are the ones that feel like real products: feeds, notifications, chat, search, and file services. These systems combine the building blocks from earlier lessons into something realistic.
list: Feeds mix read-heavy access patterns with write-heavy updates.
Notifications often rely on asynchronous workers and retry-safe delivery.
Chat systems require low latency, ordering, durable history, and reliable message delivery.
Search requires indexing, ranking, and low-latency retrieval from large data sets.
paragraphs: Feeds are a classic example of the difference between synchronous and asynchronous work. Users expect the timeline to be fast, but generating it for millions of users often requires batching, fan-out, and background processing.

Search and chat systems show the same truth in another way: a product is only as good as the architecture behind it. Success depends on indexing, latency, resilience, and ability to handle concurrent readers and writers.

This lesson is where theory becomes product intuition. You begin to see that architecture is not a collection of unrelated patterns—it is a consistent way of thinking about workload, data flow, and system behavior.

visuals.code:
flowchart TD
A[User action] --> B[Write service]
B --> C[Queue]
C --> D[Fan-out workers]
D --> E[Feed cache]
A --> F[Read API]
F --> G[Timeline store]

codeBlocks:
# Feed update flow
create_post(user, content)
  -> write to posts table
  -> enqueue feed update job
  -> fan-out to followers
  -> cache latest timeline entries

# Chat flow
message sent
  -> push to message queue
  -> persist to chat store
  -> send to recipient sessions
  -> update delivery state

sections.label: Practice
sections.title: Capstone: architect a realistic product end to end
sections.intro: Now bring everything together. Your job is not to produce one perfect answer, but to show a strong design process that can handle ambiguity, scale, and trade-offs with clarity.
sections.challenge: Design a platform that supports a large user base, stores user-generated content, handles media uploads, and preserves low-latency reads while remaining resilient during partial outages and traffic spikes.
paragraphs: This capstone is where the course becomes practical. You should be able to discuss the product flow, estimate the scale, choose the right services, identify bottlenecks, and explain why your architecture stays maintainable under growth.
A strong final answer is not the longest one. It is the one that is structured, explicit about assumptions, honest about trade-offs, and clear about what would change when the product grows further.
codeBlocks:
Capstone answer structure
1. Clarify scope and constraints
2. Estimate traffic and storage
3. Choose key services
4. Define API and data flows
5. Explain caching and consistency
6. Discuss failures, scaling, and trade-offs
